title: Where Joy, Justice, and Black Language Meet: (Re)Claiming Foundational Literacy Instruction as a Site for Transformative Possibilities
text_snippet: Where Joy, Justice, and Black Language Meet: (Re)Claiming Foundational Literacy Instruction as a Site for Transformative Possibilities ABSTRACT Phonemic awareness is a critical component of foundational literacy instruction, yet its implementation often reflects white monolingual norms and reinforces anti‐Blackness. Illustrated through a classroom vignette, this article highlights how phonemic awareness tasks can misidentify Black Language as error. Grounded in linguistic justice and pro‐Blackness, I present a reflective framework to support teachers in (re)examining task design, student responses, and instructional decisions. Through this lens, educators can affirm Black students' linguistic practices, metalinguistic awareness, and design phonemic awareness instruction that sustains their linguistic genius. By (re)claiming foundational literacy as a site for transformative possibilities, educators can foster equitable literacy learning environments that cultivate linguistic security and intellectual confidence.

title: Linguistically and Culturally Responsive Reading Conversations: Understanding and Fostering Children's Reading Engagement
text_snippet: Linguistically and Culturally Responsive Reading Conversations: Understanding and Fostering Children's Reading Engagement ABSTRACT Reading engagement is a key factor in children's literacy development, yet it often receives limited attention in classroom practice. Linguistically diverse learners may face added challenges when formal reading education and assessment focus only on the language(s) of schooling. Understanding reading engagement across its behavioral, cognitive, affective, and social dimensions helps teachers see how learners interact with and respond to texts and identify where additional support could strengthen both literacy skills and engagement. In this article, we introduce Linguistically & Culturally Responsive Reading Conversations , an Assessment for Learning approach developed and piloted with seven teachers and 38 learners aged 4–11, across four primary schools in the Netherlands and Australia. This approach treats home languages and cultural knowledge as assets, giving teachers a fuller picture of learners' reading engagement. We share practical strategies, including for teachers who do not speak or understand learners' home languages. In doing so, we show how valuing and capitalizing on learners' home languages and cultural backgrounds can also support their enjoyment of readi

title: Pedagogical Translanguaging Read‐Alouds: Making Hidden Comprehension Audible in Multilingual L2 Classrooms
text_snippet: Pedagogical Translanguaging Read‐Alouds: Making Hidden Comprehension Audible in Multilingual L2 Classrooms ABSTRACT This article reports on a translanguaging‐oriented read‐aloud implemented in a Malaysian primary classroom where pupils learned English as a second/foreign language (L2) but came from multilingual backgrounds. We observed that English‐ready pupils tended to dominate whole‐class talk, while other pupils showed understanding only through writing or in their home or first languages. To address this display‐language problem, we inserted a brief, teacher‐led multilingual turn at pre‐identified comprehension points, followed immediately by revoicing into instructional English and a return to the text. The routine was organized around four principles, namely text centrality, pre‐performance sequencing, visible teacher mediation, and English residue, so that multilingual processing advanced, rather than replaced, L2 literacy goals. Across lessons, participation widened, text‐related inferences became audible, and the subsequent English round was easier to populate. We argue that this design helps teachers reconcile equity and L2 exposure, and we offer a stepwise guide for adapting it to other multilingual literacy settings.

title: “The Rio Grande Was Originally Known as Rio Bravo”: Multiliteracies in a 4th‐Grade ELA and Social Studies Project
text_snippet: “The Rio Grande Was Originally Known as Rio Bravo”: Multiliteracies in a 4th‐Grade ELA and Social Studies Project ABSTRACT Despite the natural interdisciplinary nature of English language arts (ELA) and social studies, these two subject areas are sometimes isolated from one another in schools, including upper elementary classrooms. In this research‐in‐action article, we—two university researchers, one classroom teacher, and two undergraduate students at the time of the study—demonstrate an interdisciplinary fourth‐grade ELA and social studies project. Focusing on their favorite places in their hometown, students collaboratively constructed multimedia videos, using co‐written opinion scripts and film‐making technologies like iMovie. We examine the project through a culturally sustaining and funds of knowledge theoretical framework, analyzing how students' multiliteracies and enjoyment supported their construction of this interdisciplinary project. By emphasizing students' prior knowledge and multiliteracies, we offer one way ELA teachers might form an interdisciplinary, culturally sustaining project centered in students' enjoyment and in literacy and social studies pedagogy.

title: Supporting Students' Emotional Well‐Being and Writing Development Through Gratitude Journaling
text_snippet: Supporting Students' Emotional Well‐Being and Writing Development Through Gratitude Journaling ABSTRACT This article describes the use of gratitude journaling as a social emotional learning intervention in a kindergarten classroom. Implementation strategies and benefits of the intervention are discussed.

title: Negotiating Translanguaging in the Dual Language Bilingual Education Classroom: Supporting Latiné Students' Linguistic Intuitiveness
text_snippet: Negotiating Translanguaging in the Dual Language Bilingual Education Classroom: Supporting Latiné Students' Linguistic Intuitiveness ABSTRACT This article examines how one second‐grade dual‐language teacher supported translanguaging during interactive read‐alouds and literacy discussions while working in a district that emphasized the use of separate languages. Drawing on classroom observations, interviews, and field notes, we illustrate how the teacher encouraged students to use their bilingual resources to participate, construct meaning, and discuss texts. The findings show how translanguaging, language ideologies, and broader raciolinguistic assumptions intersected during classroom interactions and how intentional teacher responses disrupted language policing while affirming students' bilingualism. We conclude with practical recommendations for literacy educators seeking to create more linguistically just and participatory classrooms.

title: What It Truly Means To be Multilingual: Affirming Kyopomal Over “Konglish” in Early Childhood Translanguaging
text_snippet: What It Truly Means To be Multilingual: Affirming Kyopomal Over “Konglish” in Early Childhood Translanguaging ABSTRACT In bi‐/multi‐lingual and Two‐Way Immersion (TWI) programs, strict language‐separation policies often inadvertently marginalize the natural, fluid communication of emergent multilinguals, reducing their complex hybrid talk. Bridging the author's lived experience as a multilingual child with qualitative classroom research of first‐grade Korean–English students, this article challenges the monolingual gaze. Utilizing translanguaging as an overarching framework and Hybrid Semiotic Practice (HSP) as an analytical lens, the study documents how children strategically deploy their full linguistic, cultural, and embodied repertoires in peer interactions. The findings reframe these highly metacognitive, audience‐aware, and rule‐governed practices not as errors, but as Kyopomal—an agentive, community‐normed linguistic repertoire. By shifting the paradigm from “Konglish” to Kyopomal, this article offers actionable pedagogical implications for elementary literacy instruction, including cross‐linguistic wordplay. This research demonstrates that affirming these hybrid literacies is not merely an instructional scaffold, but an act of sociolinguistic justice that celebrates what it truly m

title: Using Texts as Megaphones: The Power of African American Readers Hearing Themselves in Books
text_snippet: Using Texts as Megaphones: The Power of African American Readers Hearing Themselves in Books ABSTRACT This article highlights the power of authentic children's literature to affirm African American English as a legitimate, rule‐governed linguistic system and elevate it as a source of cognitive strength, cultural richness, and academic potential. While foundational literacy skills emphasize English language structure, they often center General American English and overlook the linguistic realities of many African American students. As a result, traditional literacy instruction can marginalize Black students by framing their home language as a deficit rather than a resource. Authentic children's literature featuring AAE validates African American students' identities where their voices can be celebrated in the classroom. This article calls for the intentional use of authentic literature to affirm students' primary language. It provides research‐based strategies that foster literacy development and build linguistic pride. By merging AAE‐rich literature with culturally responsive practices, educators can create classrooms that center students' full linguistic repertoires as assets for learning and meaning‐making.

title: “ Walk It Like You Talk It! ” the Freedom School National Training as a Cultural Immersion Experience for Preservice Teachers Grappling With Understanding the Intersections of Culturally Relevant Teaching and Social Justice in Literacy Education
text_snippet: “ Walk It Like You Talk It! ” the Freedom School National Training as a Cultural Immersion Experience for Preservice Teachers Grappling With Understanding the Intersections of Culturally Relevant Teaching and Social Justice in Literacy Education ABSTRACT This qualitative critical case study investigates how preservice teachers (PSTs) working within Freedom School (FS) (a national K‐12 six‐week summer and afterschool literacy program) develop an understanding of social justice, culturally relevant teaching (CRT), and conceptions of literacy development, as well as explores the impact of them attending the Children's Defense Fund Freedom Schools Program (CDF FSP) National Training (NT). According to research, there is a need for PST programs to prepare educators using CRT approaches. Researchers utilized reflexive thematic analysis to analyze observational and interview data collected from 4 PSTs before, during, and after the CDF FSP NT. Findings revealed PSTs gained a deeper understanding of CRT, social justice, and students' literacy assets. This research informs teacher educators about ways to engage PSTs in more meaningful and authentic experiences, specifically within literacy instruction. title: Living Comics: Playful and Embodied Composing With Emergent Bilingual Learners
text_snippet: Living Comics: Playful and Embodied Composing With Emergent Bilingual Learners ABSTRACT There is evidence to support that the diverse linguistic repertoire of emergent bilingual students enhances learning and development. Multimodal composing offers a unique opportunity for teachers to design lessons that draw upon emergent bilinguals' knowledge through visual means, without necessarily requiring advanced English proficiency. In the proposed activity, “Living Comics,” emergent bilingual students embody a comic character's physical expression then use visual elements to expand a storytelling frame. This activity leverages multimodal ways of understanding and composing a text, so that students can express their comprehension and ideas more confidently. In the article, we outline the purpose, objective, and benefits of this engaging whole‐group activity. Furthermore, we lay out the steps needed for teachers to reproduce and contextualize “Living Comics” in their own classrooms.

title: Collective Knowing, Collective Growing: Centering Families in Virtual Literacy Work
text_snippet: Collective Knowing, Collective Growing: Centering Families in Virtual Literacy Work ABSTRACT Roc Reading Partners (RRP) grew from the belief that when children feel joy and connection, they thrive as readers (Muhammad 2020). What began as a pandemic‐era initiative has evolved into a university supported, community rooted model for equitable literacy engagement, designed to address resource inequities in districts where economic disparities limit access to age‐appropriate reading materials (Neuman and Celano 2012). This teaching and learning guide frames literacy as a social and relational process (Gee 2004; Heath 1983; Street 1984, 2008), positioning families as Co‐pedagogical partners. Grounded in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy (Ladson‐Billings 1995, 2021) and informed by culturally and linguistically sustaining practices (Paris and Alim 2014), RRP centers joy as the heartbeat of learning (Muhammad 2020). The program utilizes structured accountability tools including culturally relevant implementation checklists and student‐led choice boards to curate identity affirming, culturally rooted literacy experiences. Nightly zoom‐based sessions incorporate micro‐professional development for tutors with continuous feedback loops that sustain high‐fidelity implementation an

title: Using the Identify, Instruct, Incorporate (3‐I) Framework to Teach Graphical Literacy Skills
text_snippet: Using the Identify, Instruct, Incorporate (3‐I) Framework to Teach Graphical Literacy Skills ABSTRACT Graphical literacy, the ability to read, interpret, and create graphics, is essential for whole‐text comprehension, especially when reading informational texts, including children's magazines. Our research examined the graphics ( n = 416) in a popular children's magazine, Scholastic News ( N = 30), for graphic category, type, function, and connection to text. Our findings showed that most graphics are representational photographs and general images that connect easily to the main text. Some graphics were more complex and may require explicit instruction. We also found an increase in infographics, both those associated with an article and those as the main article. Based on our findings, we propose the 3‐I framework (Identify, Instruct, Incorporate) to guide teachers' graphical literacy instruction.

title: Augmenting Literacy Instruction With Strategies Connected to Expanding Views
text_snippet: Augmenting Literacy Instruction With Strategies Connected to Expanding Views ABSTRACT Recent policies in education have prompted the implementation of scripted core literacy programs, resulting in increased teacher‐directed, systematic phonics instruction. While such shifts support a simplified view of reading, more than 1/3 of students continue to experience reading difficulties, prompting consideration of relying on a single method of teaching reading. Expanding views draw attention to tending to necessary bridging processes, self‐regulatory behaviors, and cultural and asset‐based pedagogies within reading instruction. As educators determine the best combination of methods for teaching students at the emergent and early reading stages, augmenting structured literacy programming with play‐based strategies that foster student dialogue around the concept of word in text (COW‐T) may support sensemaking and cognitive flexibility needed to become proficient readers and move beyond rote skill practice. Additionally, strategic selection of texts can offer various opportunities to connect students' funds of knowledge and cultural assets or reinforce critical academic content. title: Rehearsing Responsiveness: Coaching Preservice Teachers to Work Within and Beyond Standardized Lesson Plans
text_snippet: Rehearsing Responsiveness: Coaching Preservice Teachers to Work Within and Beyond Standardized Lesson Plans ABSTRACT Centrally developed English lesson plans provide structure and ensure curriculum coverage, yet they can constrain preservice teachers' creativity, responsiveness, and capacity to engage students meaningfully. Although this tension is well documented, there is limited practical guidance for teacher educators in University Teacher Preparation Programs. This article addresses this gap by sharing practical strategies grounded in theory and existing research through a practitioner inquiry. This inquiry examines how coaching, framed by Wassermann's idea of the organic literacy classroom, supports preservice teachers in working within and beyond standardized curriculum materials. Drawing on survey data, alongside observational and reflective data generated from university tutorials and school‐based experiences, the article illustrates how coaching and rehearsal with Year 1 English lesson plans enable preservice teachers to identify pedagogical entry points for responsive, student‐centered teaching. In doing so, the article offers practice‐based insights for teacher educators, demonstrating how prescriptive materials can be worked with—rather than resisted—to create opportunities

title: “Kids Don't Know Where to Look!”: Using Think‐Alouds to Teach Students to Interpret Diagrams
text_snippet: “Kids Don't Know Where to Look!”: Using Think‐Alouds to Teach Students to Interpret Diagrams ABSTRACT Elementary students frequently encounter diagrams and flowcharts in science texts, yet many engage with them only at a surface level. They can identify labels or colors but struggle to understand how visual features work together to convey meaning. This article introduces multiple visual literacy strategies that teachers can model through think‐alouds to help both native English speakers and multilingual students interpret and integrate information from scientific diagrams. Drawing on classroom‐based examples from grades 3–5, the article provides ready‐to‐use lesson plans, teacher scripts, and student artifacts that demonstrate how these strategies, such as interpreting graphics, connecting graphics to text, and making inferential descriptions, can be embedded within existing science instruction. These examples offer teachers concrete tools to help students read diagrams as meaning‐making systems, fostering both science understanding and visual literacy.

title: Little Letters, Heavy Lessons: A Black Mother's Critique of a “Simple” Phonics Lesson and the Myths of Neutral Instruction
text_snippet: Little Letters, Heavy Lessons: A Black Mother's Critique of a “Simple” Phonics Lesson and the Myths of Neutral Instruction ABSTRACT Racialized multilingual children need their cultural and linguistic sophistication to be seen and heard in their classrooms. Drawing from my daughter's first grade educational experiences, this article explores how the teaching of a popular phonics‐based sorting lesson centered around the pronunciation of the inflectional suffix “‐ed” became an unintentional site of anti‐Blackness, even in a school that purported to center and celebrate linguistic diversity and social justice. Using a BlackCrit analysis of the lesson and a Black feminist Motherwork reflection on my conversations with my daughter's teachers, I highlight how White Mainstream English was foregrounded in the teaching, assessment, and justification of the lesson. I suggest approaches to teaching elementary‐aged children the dynamic nature of the pronunciation of the inflectional suffix “‐ed” that celebrate and justly center the use of Black languages.

title: More Than a Name: Identity, Culture, and Representation in Children's Picturebooks
text_snippet: More Than a Name: Identity, Culture, and Representation in Children's Picturebooks ABSTRACT This article explores how names, name stories, and naming picturebooks affirm children's identities and foster inclusive classroom environments. Drawing on interviews with seven cultural insiders, educators from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds, the study examines real‐life naming experiences alongside representations in multicultural picturebooks. Through grounded theory methods, employing open coding and thematic analysis, the findings highlight the emotional and cultural significance of names and the consequences of mispronunciation or name alteration in educational settings. Picturebooks such as Becoming Vanessa and Say My Name serve as critical tools for identity affirmation, empathy, and teaching students about names. Pedagogical implications for using naming stories in early childhood and elementary classrooms include emphasizing culturally sustaining practices, read‐alouds, and community building to honor every child's name and background.

title: Co‐Designing Multimodal, Multilingual Text Sets: Centering Caregiver Choice
text_snippet: Co‐Designing Multimodal, Multilingual Text Sets: Centering Caregiver Choice ABSTRACT Early literacy instruction in the U.S. often centers monolingual, English‐dominant practices that marginalize multilingual learners and their families. This qualitative design‐based research study examines a family literacy initiative that engaged caregivers and teachers as co‐designers of a multilingual, multimodal literacy resource bag. Using the MultiSemiotic Architecture Framework, we analyzed qualitative data to explore how collaborative text selection can advance linguistic justice in early childhood education. Findings highlight five themes that shaped intentional text selection and supported multilingual home literacy practices: content, language, cultural relevance, curricular alignment, and collaborative modifications. By centering families' cultural and linguistic resources, the project disrupted monolingual norms and cultivated partnerships that bridged school and home literacies. The study offers practical implications for educators and researchers seeking to design family literacy initiatives that sustain home languages and affirm multilingual families' expertise.

title: “I'ma Superhero Too.”: A Critical Case Study of a Black Student's Biliteracy Journey
text_snippet: “I'ma Superhero Too.”: A Critical Case Study of a Black Student's Biliteracy Journey ABSTRACT This article explores the biliteracy journey of Jamaal, an African American, in an elementary dual language bilingual education (DLBE) classroom. Although scholars have researched the biliteracy development and identity construction of bilingual children for decades, limited research has explored the biliteracy trajectory of African Americans in DLBE, including how they maintain biliteracy identities while also resisting historical stigmatization of their linguistic practices. This qualitative study draws upon raciolinguistic perspectives, translanguaging, and liberation literacies. These theoretical lenses provide a foundation to explore the complexity of how African American children navigate racialized biliteracy development in DLBE and illuminate the fullness of their linguistic repertoires. Data were collected from an ethnographic case study in a Midwestern elementary DLBE program primarily serving Latine/x and African American children. Findings demonstrate how African American children are capable of employing their linguistic resources for linguistic liberation. title: Is ‘Typically Developing’ Really Typical? Reimagining Deaf Literacies Through Crip Linguistics
text_snippet: Is ‘Typically Developing’ Really Typical? Reimagining Deaf Literacies Through Crip Linguistics ABSTRACT Crip linguistics is a philosophical framework for considering how various people with different access and experiences (e.g., deaf individuals, people with diagnosed language disabilities, DeafBlind people) use language. This framework is asset‐based and assumes that language differences are not language disorders. In this Viewpoints article, we explore the literacy development of those with language differences from a Crip linguistics perspective. We argue that various ways of being literate have inherent value, and should not inherently be considered as disabilities or disorders in need of remediation. We provide recommendations for teachers working with students with language differences, including exposing children to language varieties, providing opportunities for meaningful engagement with print, broadening text exposure, and rethinking assessment practices.

title: Toward Linguistic Justice: Immigrant Students' and Families' Languaging as Pedagogical Disruption of School‐Based Literacy Instruction
text_snippet: Toward Linguistic Justice: Immigrant Students' and Families' Languaging as Pedagogical Disruption of School‐Based Literacy Instruction ABSTRACT In this article, we examine immigrant families' language and literacy practices against the backdrop of school‐based literacy instruction in two dual language bilingual education (DLBE) programs: Vietnamese/English and Portuguese/English. We draw upon raciolinguistics and translanguaging scholarship to analyze interviews, classroom observations, and home visits to five Vietnamese families and five Brazilian families whose children attended the DLBE programs in the same state. Our findings highlight that families' language and literacy practices were often devalued as “inappropriate” and “uneducated” in schools despite serving as rich cultural and linguistic resources in multilingual students' everyday lives. We also document the transnational, translingual, and multimodal literacies that immigrant families cultivated across home, community, and transnational contexts. Although situated within DLBE contexts, these findings have broad implications for educators who serve multilingual learners in both bilingual and English‐medium classrooms. We argue that diversifying literacy instruction requires critical listening and equitable family engagement to honor linguistic sovereig

title: Balancing the Chalk and the Check: Teacher Autonomy Amid the Rise of Scripted Reading Programs
text_snippet: Balancing the Chalk and the Check: Teacher Autonomy Amid the Rise of Scripted Reading Programs ABSTRACT Phonics is widely acknowledged in the research literature as an essential element of learning to read, but the effectiveness of various commercial programs for improving reading outcomes remains a subject of ongoing debate in research and the media. This study explores the delicate balance between teacher autonomy and scripted reading programs by surveying Australian elementary teachers' reported practices and perspectives regarding their teaching autonomy amid the use of commercial reading programs in their classrooms. Consideration is given to how teachers can be supported in developing their professional knowledge, judgment, and autonomy alongside the use of evidence‐based practices for reading instruction in the early years of schooling.

title: Raciolinguistic Autobiographies With Intermediate Elementary Learners
text_snippet: Raciolinguistic Autobiographies With Intermediate Elementary Learners ABSTRACT We propose raciolinguistic autobiographies as a developmentally appropriate multimodal composition authored by intermediate elementary learners (Grades 3–5) that promotes critical consciousness around how language, race, and signs are interwoven to form hierarchies of power and belonging. We provide learning objectives, concrete pedagogical strategies, and examples that educators can implement in their intermediate elementary classrooms. The pedagogical outline is informed by raciolinguistic and raciosemiotic perspectives. Raciolinguistic autobiographie s provide crucial tools for [minoritized] young learners to denaturalize the raciolinguistic and raciosemiotic signs that seek to devalue them, their communities, and their practices of belonging.

title: Giving Voice to Wordless Picture Books: A Teaching Tip
text_snippet: Giving Voice to Wordless Picture Books: A Teaching Tip ABSTRACT This article shares a teaching tip that helps students actively engage in giving voice to wordless picture books. It begins with a vignette that became the impetus for writing this article. Next, it provides important background information about the benefits of wordless picture books. Then, it describes and illustrates a teaching tip that teachers can use with younger and older readers. It ends with lessons learned and suggestions for moving forward with wordless picture books.

title: Zoom In and Zoom Out: (Re)Telling Our Cultural Literacy Practices Through Engaged Learning
text_snippet: Zoom In and Zoom Out: (Re)Telling Our Cultural Literacy Practices Through Engaged Learning ABSTRACT Empowering bilingual learners to engage in the Zoom In and Zoom Out approach is a way to enrich and validate students' cultural identity and support students' linguistic and academic development while fostering rich writing opportunities for students. Teachers will discover a genuine way that empowers students to explore vocabulary, build comprehension, and acquire a love for writing. This effective multifaceted strategy approaches writing by leveraging students' cultural background and literacy practices. Students will capitalize on their funds of knowledge and use their experiences to further propel their writing efforts. By starting from within, diverse learners make stronger connections with the academic setting. Integrating this culturally sustaining pedagogical approach will enrich diverse learners' cultural and linguistic identities.

title: Beyond Mechanics: How Multilingual Kindergarteners Make Meaning in Writing
text_snippet: Beyond Mechanics: How Multilingual Kindergarteners Make Meaning in Writing ABSTRACT Kindergarten multilingual learners (MLs) convey rich meaning through multimodal writing, drawing on a range of linguistic and visual resources that can easily be overlooked when teachers limit their focus to the mechanics of a child's writing. Looking beyond mechanical features of writing helps teachers understand the complexity of how MLs convey meaning, drawing on a range of semiotic tools in their early writing.

title: They Don't Talk Very Good: Attending to Raciolinguistic Socialization in Early Childhood
text_snippet: They Don't Talk Very Good: Attending to Raciolinguistic Socialization in Early Childhood ABSTRACT In this article, I share experiences from my roles as a teacher, researcher, and parent to show how raciolinguistic ideologies take hold in early childhood. Specifically, I illustrate how children come to uphold English superiority, map language to belonging, and make judgments about whose language counts. In sharing these experiences, I call on educators and caregivers to attend to raciolinguistic socialization and work toward disruption so that all children's languages are valued in literacy learning. I suggest centering multiple languages, cultivating curiosity, and questioning curricular assumptions as ways to work alongside children in challenging hierarchies and creating learning spaces that honor the multilingual world in which we live.

title: Text Development for an Open‐Access Elementary Science Curriculum: Five Principles for Supporting the Use of Science Text
text_snippet: Text Development for an Open‐Access Elementary Science Curriculum: Five Principles for Supporting the Use of Science Text ABSTRACT Integrating science and literacy in elementary education enhances student learning. Curriculum materials play a key role in providing teachers with resources and texts that support this integration. This paper presents five principles for using science texts to support science and literacy learning in elementary classrooms. The paper describes how these principles were applied to create over 200 texts for a free, open‐access science curriculum. We emphasize how teachers can put these principles into practice to support elementary literacy and science learning. Two years of field testing with over 550 teachers and 20,000 elementary students across nine states demonstrated the feasibility of using these texts within the OpenSciEd Elementary curriculum. Teachers reported that the texts embedded within the curriculum deepened students' scientific knowledge, expanded students' vocabulary, and helped students connect their science learning to real‐world contexts.

title: Decolonizing Literacy: A Black SLP's Journey to Centering Diverse Linguistic Practices in Reading Instruction
text_snippet: Decolonizing Literacy: A Black SLP's Journey to Centering Diverse Linguistic Practices in Reading Instruction ABSTRACT This article explores how centering Black Language within reading instruction can transform early literacy outcomes and affirm student identity. Written from the perspective of a Black, bidialectal speech‐language pathologist (SLP), the piece challenges traditional, corrective models of literacy by highlighting the pedagogical power of Black Language. Drawing on Black Language, linguistic justice, and literacy scholarship, the article presents classroom‐ready practices—such as metalinguistic awareness activities, culturally relevant read‐alouds, code‐meshing awareness, and phonological instruction grounded in students' native language—that affirm linguistic sovereignty and enhance engagement. Through narrative reflection, instructional examples, and student responses, the article illustrates how SLPs and educators can collaboratively implement linguistically affirming practices that reframe dominant language ideologies. Incorporating Black Language is not simply an instructional choice—it is a justice‐oriented stance that reimagines literacy as a site of empowerment, belonging, and cultural pride.

title: Loving, Luchando, and Literacy: Bilingual Latinx Mothers and the Power of Testimonios in a Community Book Club
text_snippet: Loving, Luchando, and Literacy: Bilingual Latinx Mothers and the Power of Testimonios in a Community Book Club ABSTRACT This study explores how bilingual Latinx mothers engage in storytelling as a powerful form of familial and cultural literacy. Drawing from sociocultural theory, community cultural wealth, and translanguaging, the research centers a six‐week bilingual summer book club for mothers and their children. Through cuentos and testimonios, the mothers articulated themes of language, love, and luchando (striving), using multimodal and translingual storytelling to affirm cultural identity, resist deficit narratives, and transmit intergenerational knowledge. These narratives positioned mothers not only as caregivers but as pedagogical leaders, challenging narrow definitions of literacy and offering alternative frameworks rooted in emotional labor, cultural memory, and relational teaching. Findings highlight how literacy, when rooted in community and love, becomes a tool for healing, resistance, and reimagining educational spaces. This research affirms the critical role of Latinx mothers as storytellers, educators, and cultural workers, expanding the field's understanding of where and how literacy happens.

title: I Need More Than WCPM! The Word Recognition Record (WR 2 )
text_snippet: I Need More Than WCPM! The Word Recognition Record (WR 2 ) ABSTRACT Using an assessment that provides a WCPM score is a necessary, useful, and efficient way to monitor and evaluate students' progress in their reading development. But WCPM does not provide diagnostic information of instructional value to teachers. Adding WR 2 to the administration of 1‐min fluency probes (OMFP) allows teachers to track and target individual students' specific word recognition skills in real reading settings adding significant instructional value for teachers. The Word Recognition Record (WR 2 ) uses a research‐based process to analyze oral reading errors of students' 1‐min fluency probes. Based on research reported in 2026, this article describes the development and use of the WR 2 in classroom assessment settings. The WR 2 can give teachers valuable information from repeated OMFP assessments. For individual students, using the WR 2 with each OMFP helps teachers spot patterns in word recognition skills and identify areas needing more support. At the classroom level, it also helps teachers see which students share similar needs and group them for focused small‐group instruction.

title: Systematic Reading Assessment and Motivating Feedback Through the Read to Me Checklist
text_snippet: Systematic Reading Assessment and Motivating Feedback Through the Read to Me Checklist ABSTRACT Reading is fundamentally a forward‐directed act of interpretation—a process driven by anticipating and constructing meaning. Yet our systematic review of 52 studies finds that practices of feedback on early oral reading often focus disproportionately on error correction—a pattern especially pronounced for struggling and multilingual learners. In this study we take a teacher‐focused approach to using the Read To Me checklist, a research‐based tool for assessing and providing feedback on oral reading that fosters both decoding proficiency and motivation. The Read To Me checklist responds to the common feedback bias toward error correction by guiding teachers to attend to a broad range of reading skills, including decoding, motivation, and comprehension, and to use what is termed “agentic feedback” to foster both a positive reader identity and a sense of student agency. Findings show that teachers using the checklist broadened their focus beyond accuracy, attending also to interpretation and agency. In this resource, we provide practical tips and classroom vignettes that demonstrate how small shifts in feedback can support skill development while strengthening reader identity

title: An Exploration of the Use of Musical Activities to Promote Foundational Literacy Competencies for Children Aged 3–5 Years
text_snippet: An Exploration of the Use of Musical Activities to Promote Foundational Literacy Competencies for Children Aged 3–5 Years ABSTRACT Research into the process of becoming literate mainly focuses on the teaching of the alphabetic principle as a starting point upon school entry. However, experiences, knowledge, and skills prior to this point may determine future success. This research examines how musical activities may be used to foster these foundational literacy competencies. Using a micro‐ethnographic, qualitative design, this study sought to examine the extent to which a daily literacy‐through‐music program of 30–40 min duration, implemented in an area of social deprivation over a six‐week period, for a group of nine participants aged 3–5 years of age, could be successful in promoting the identified foundational literacy competencies. The findings suggested that such a program could facilitate the acquisition of these competencies and as such have unique implications for the pedagogical practice of early years practitioners in the establishing of secure literacy foundations for further formal literacy learning.

title: Building Bridges: Five Sociocultural Practices for Reading Comprehension
text_snippet: Building Bridges: Five Sociocultural Practices for Reading Comprehension ABSTRACT This article argues that decades of research provide robust evidence for a sociocultural approach to teaching reading comprehension, yet implementation of this approach has been slow and uneven. The sociocultural approach situates students' cultural, linguistic, and personal knowledge at the heart of their meaning making with texts. The article identifies five core practices that teachers can use to take advantage of these social and cultural resources. These practices include focusing on relevant and authentic reading comprehension tasks; using varied texts; supporting respectful and responsive social interactions; encouraging collaboration to deepen text understanding; and providing strategic reading comprehension support to enhance students' reading practices and develop their independence. Each practice is illustrated with research and getting started tips that show how these approaches can be enacted to transform classrooms into inclusive spaces where all learners can thrive as capable readers and meaning‐makers.

title: From Preparation to Practice: A Follow Up Study of Novice Teachers' Use of Texas Reading Academy Practices
text_snippet: From Preparation to Practice: A Follow Up Study of Novice Teachers' Use of Texas Reading Academy Practices ABSTRACT This qualitative case study examines how six first‐year teachers enacted content knowledge from the Texas Reading Academy (TRA) during their classroom teaching. Semi‐structured interviews focused on instructional decision‐making, perceived supports, and barriers to implementation. Findings indicate structured practices such as phonics and phonemic awareness routines transferred more consistently into classroom instruction, while discourse‐oriented and formative assessment practices proved more fragile and highly dependent on time, curriculum alignment, and classroom demands. Mentorship and collaborative supports facilitated enactment, whereas systemic misalignment constrained teachers' use of TRA‐aligned practices. Extending an earlier pilot study that documented preservice teachers' confidence and anticipated barriers, this follow‐up investigation highlights both the durability and fragility of TRA knowledge in practice and situates Texas within a broader national discussion of the challenges associated with sustaining science of reading reforms during teachers' early careers.

title: Introducing the Record of Decision‐Making: A New Formative Assessment for Oral Reading
text_snippet: Introducing the Record of Decision‐Making: A New Formative Assessment for Oral Reading ABSTRACT In this “Teaching and Learning in Practice” article, we introduce the record of decision‐making (RODM), a formative assessment of decoding while reading that measures the frequency of a student's use of backup strategies while reading aloud. We first explain backup strategies and then share validation and reliability evidence for the backup strategies that we include on the RODM. We also describe how to administer and interpret the results. At the end of the article, we provide a link to free, asynchronous training materials.

title: Authors as Mentors: Grammar as Tools, Not Rules
text_snippet: Authors as Mentors: Grammar as Tools, Not Rules ABSTRACT Using a contextualized approach to grammar instruction, with published authors as mentors, contrasts starkly to ineffective methods that use worksheets and isolated grammar instruction. With this contextualized approach, students turn to authors as mentors for using grammar as tools, not rules. Positioning published authors as mentors for students' writing provides authentic models for students to construct knowledge about grammar within meaningful contexts. This article offers a process for using mentor texts as a pathway for teaching grammar and usage. We include both primary grade and middle‐school examples of this approach, which offers a research‐based alternative to ineffective grammar instruction that is driven by worksheets and decontextualized examples.

title: Building Knowledge, Building Minds: How Content‐Rich Instruction Matters for Vocabulary and Reading Comprehension
text_snippet: Building Knowledge, Building Minds: How Content‐Rich Instruction Matters for Vocabulary and Reading Comprehension ABSTRACT This article makes the case for building knowledge as a central component of early literacy instruction. Drawing from classroom observations and research‐based practices, it emphasizes that comprehension is not a generic skill but is deeply tied to content knowledge and vocabulary. The article highlights key design features for knowledge‐building, including the use of topics, content‐rich vocabulary, and scaffolded questioning to foster deeper understanding. It argues that knowledge should be interconnected, culturally inclusive, and engaging—helping all children to think critically and make meaningful connections. By ensuring shared knowledge among students, educators can reduce disparities and create a more equitable learning environment where every child has the opportunity to succeed.

title: Bilingual Literacy Curricula for Bilingual Deaf Students
text_snippet: Bilingual Literacy Curricula for Bilingual Deaf Students ABSTRACT There is often a disconnect between the reading curriculum used in public schools with hearing students and what best practice suggests for bilingual deaf students (students who use American Sign Language (ASL) and print and/or spoken English). In this article, we explore a deaf education teacher's first‐time use of two curricula designed specifically for deaf students who use ASL: the Bedrock Literacy Curriculum and the Bilingual Grammar Curriculum. This journey is chronicled through the teacher's perception of her implementation and her elementary students' responses to instruction. After sharing students' academic progress and the influence the use of these curricula had on students' self‐concept, we describe challenges encountered during a year of implementation with these two curricula. Finally, we offer our interpretations and recommendations for others who are teaching literacy skills to young deaf students.

title: The Effectiveness of Explicit Vocabulary Instruction for Bilingual Autistic Children
text_snippet: The Effectiveness of Explicit Vocabulary Instruction for Bilingual Autistic Children ABSTRACT Increasing vocabulary is of fundamental importance for helping multilingual children reach proficiency in English, yet children with additional learning challenges such as speech delay and autism spectrum disorder have extra difficulty in this area. Previous research found that meaningful repetition and explicit vocabulary instruction are effective strategies that allow children to learn words that would normally be considered beyond their developmental level. This pilot study examines vocabulary gains made over one month by eight bilingual children, including three diagnosed with autism, following the combined strategies of meaningful repetition and explicit vocabulary instruction using visuals in teaching advanced vocabulary words. Results are measured by a picture‐cued multiple‐choice assessment. A 37.5% increase in the average score compared to pretest scores indicates that these strategies are indeed effective for bilingual students with speech delay and autism. A literature review and discussion of the findings includes consideration of implications for pedagogy and language assessment.

title: Enhancing Prekindergarten Narrative Skills Through Picturebook Art Exploration
text_snippet: Enhancing Prekindergarten Narrative Skills Through Picturebook Art Exploration ABSTRACT Prekindergarten students participated in illustration analysis during an afterschool art club, demonstrating approaches adaptable across diverse educational contexts globally. Each day the teacher utilized seminar approaches to connect the illustrations to key elements of narrative discourse structures, such as setting, character, emotions, the passage of time, problem and solution, prediction, and inference. In addition, in each session students created and narrated their own illustrations. Participants in the art club significantly increased their oral narrative ability, language complexity, narrative retelling, story comprehension, vocabulary usage, and episodic components.

title: Learning About the Acadian Deportation Through Children's Literature
text_snippet: Learning About the Acadian Deportation Through Children's Literature ABSTRACT The purpose of this Teaching and Learning Guide is to provide perspective on addressing the difficult topic of deportation of an ethnic group while using children's literature as a guide; we also aim to model evidence‐based reading comprehension strategies such as activating prior knowledge and making text‐to‐self connections.

title: Combatting Curriculum Violence: Historical Fiction Text Selection Through the Lens of the Black Girls' Literacies Framework
text_snippet: Combatting Curriculum Violence: Historical Fiction Text Selection Through the Lens of the Black Girls' Literacies Framework ABSTRACT This paper presents a critical content analysis of middle grade books featuring Black girls before the end of the Civil War, aiming to guide the selection of culturally relevant classroom texts. Using the Black Girls' Literacy Framework, we examined how each book represented key elements beyond simply featuring a Black female protagonist. Findings emphasize the importance of texts that challenge dominant narratives and reflect students' multiple literacies and identities. We conclude with recommendations for teachers to analyze texts and design curricula that honor the diverse experiences students bring to the classroom.

title: From Policing to Sustaining Black Language: Decolonizing Oral Reading Assessments and Advancing Linguistic Justice
text_snippet: From Policing to Sustaining Black Language: Decolonizing Oral Reading Assessments and Advancing Linguistic Justice ABSTRACT This article argues for the urgent need to reframe oral reading assessments through a lens of linguistic justice by centering Black Language as a sophisticated linguistic system within a decolonizing framework. Despite rhetorical claims of honoring linguistic diversity, assessment practices often demand assimilation to standardized English, perpetuating colonial and deficit‐oriented ideologies. Drawing on translanguaging theory as a decolonizing project, the article demonstrates how features of Black Language in oral reading reflect students' active meaning‐making and should be recognized as strengths in reading development rather than treated as errors. Through analysis of assessment practices, raciolinguistic ideologies, and historical contexts, I examine the harm caused when Black Language goes unacknowledged and offer concrete pathways for educators to move from deficit‐oriented evaluation toward linguistically sustaining practice. The article concludes with five decolonizing paradigm shifts spanning assessment, classroom instruction, multimodal representation, and teacher education, moving educators from policing to sustaining Black Language.

title: Put Aside Your Pencil: How Talk Becomes Writing Through Verbal Rehearsal
text_snippet: Put Aside Your Pencil: How Talk Becomes Writing Through Verbal Rehearsal ABSTRACT Writing is essential in both academic and professional settings. Yet, becoming an expert writer is challenging, and teachers need ways to support students' growth as writers. This article explores how teachers can use verbal rehearsal, an oral writing intervention, to enhance the quality of students' initial drafts. One student's writing will be highlighted to demonstrate how verbal rehearsal was used, which resulted in progress toward an organized and elaborated first draft. The aim is to provide teachers with insights into implementing verbal rehearsal in classrooms to improve writing instruction.

title: From Silence to Story: A Practical Guide to Implementing Modeled Sustained Silent Reading ( MSSR ) in Our Early Childhood Classrooms and Homes
text_snippet: From Silence to Story: A Practical Guide to Implementing Modeled Sustained Silent Reading ( MSSR ) in Our Early Childhood Classrooms and Homes ABSTRACT Faced with the challenge of fostering genuine literacy engagement amidst curriculum demands and digital distractions, our “Reading for Tomorrow” initiative in Taiwan turned to Modeled Sustained Silent Reading (MSSR) as a cornerstone practice. This article offers a practical guide based on our experiences implementing MSSR across 30 diverse kindergartens. It explains the motivation for our book‐focused approach and then details how we cultivated immersive reading environments, structured daily reading routines, and facilitated rich book talks in our classrooms. Furthermore, we outline our strategies for transforming parent‐teacher relationships from passive communication to active co‐creation, extending reading into the home. Our goal is to offer actionable insights for fellow literacy educators and parents seeking to cultivate joyful, lifelong readers.

title: Communicative Belonging in Early Literacy: Who Is Heard, Whose Literacies Matter, and Who Belongs
text_snippet: Communicative Belonging in Early Literacy: Who Is Heard, Whose Literacies Matter, and Who Belongs ABSTRACT Early literacy teaching and learning shapes whose voices are heard, whose ways of communicating are valued, and who belongs in school. Yet, early literacy classrooms are often governed by white, monolingual norms that marginalize multilingual and multidialectal children, positioning linguistic difference as a problem. This article advances communicative belonging as a justice‐centered framework that reframes literacy from gatekeeping to a relational practice grounded in listening, affirmation, and care. We articulate four interrelated commitments—intrapersonal, interpersonal, organizational, and communal—and illustrate how teachers can activate communicative belonging by listening for meaning, inviting translanguaging, and affirming diverse literacies in everyday teaching, learning, and assessment. When early literacy is designed for belonging, it becomes a shared practice of agency, dignity, and connection.

title: Empowering Chinese American Children as Critical Readers and Agents of Diverse Children's Literature
text_snippet: Empowering Chinese American Children as Critical Readers and Agents of Diverse Children's Literature ABSTRACT This practitioner inquiry employs AsianCrit to inform both the design and analysis of two children's literature workshops, critically examining how Chinese American bi/multilingual children define and evaluate Chinese American picturebooks and envision more diverse representations. Drawing on classroom recordings, interviews, and rich artifacts, this study highlighted how Chinese American children can serve as co‐theorizers and critics of children's literature when given the opportunity to reflect on and discuss their racialized, linguistic, and transnational experiences. The study underscores the importance of actively incorporating children's perspectives into reimagining more diverse and authentic representations in children's literature. It also offers pedagogical implications for practitioners to engage in critical reflection on their own biases, employ intentional reading strategies and activities, and collaborate with local communities to shape students' experiences with literature.

title: “Wait and See” Project: Journaling and Arts‐Integration to Explore Identity With Multilingual Learners
text_snippet: “Wait and See” Project: Journaling and Arts‐Integration to Explore Identity With Multilingual Learners ABSTRACT This Teaching and Learning in Practice article describes a six‐week “Wait‐and‐See Identity Project” conducted with multilingual learners ages 9–13. Integrating identity‐based journaling and arts‐based activities, this teacher‐developed, teacher‐led project invited students to explore and negotiate aspects of their identities while engaging in meaning‐making around a shared novel. The project weaves together multimodality, student voice, and authentic literacy engagement.

title: Names Matter: Fostering Cultural Awareness Through Multimodal Literacy in a Predominantly White Classroom
text_snippet: Names Matter: Fostering Cultural Awareness Through Multimodal Literacy in a Predominantly White Classroom ABSTRACT This article demonstrates how picture books centered on names can foster cultural awareness and identity development in young children. Through a cycle of repeated read‐alouds combined with multimodal activities, including visual arts, music, crafts, and generative AI, we guided students toward personal reflection and creative expression. Our findings indicate that this approach extends classroom discussions beyond surface‐level comprehension to foster critical thinking and meaningful connections with the students' lived experiences, resulting in high levels of engagement. We provide practical strategies and classroom examples to help educators design inclusive, identity‐affirming learning experiences that honor each child's unique story about their names.

title: From Monolingualism to Plurilingualism: Multimodal Arts‐Based Cultural Probes as Catalysts for Linguistic Justice in an Afterschool Literacy Program
text_snippet: From Monolingualism to Plurilingualism: Multimodal Arts‐Based Cultural Probes as Catalysts for Linguistic Justice in an Afterschool Literacy Program ABSTRACT Afterschool programs in Anglophone Canada often reinforce monolingual English norms, marginalizing multilingual students' linguistic and cultural resources. In a research project conducted over three 16‐week cycles at two schools, we selected relevant books and actively engaged parents and students with multimodal, arts‐based cultural probes—such as collage, painting, rapping, and digital mapping—that encouraged culturally and linguistically diverse (CLD) children's reclamation of their minoritized languages, affirmed cultural identities, and confronted linguistic exclusion. Student artwork, interviews, and classroom observations showed greater use of home languages, increased pride in students' cultural backgrounds, and more resistance against linguistic and cultural exclusion compared to prior field observations. Findings suggest that these arts‐based probes not only support English literacy development but also affirm students' full linguistic and cultural identities. This work offers practical guidance for designing inclusive learning environments and highlights the importance of engaging parents in critical conversations about language, culture, and identity at home.

title: Empowering Readers: Boosting Reading Engagement for Third Graders With Book Clubs in a Rural Title 1 School
text_snippet: Empowering Readers: Boosting Reading Engagement for Third Graders With Book Clubs in a Rural Title 1 School ABSTRACT This study explores the impact of Book Clubs on reading engagement among at‐risk third‐grade students in a rural Title 1 elementary school. Grounded in Engagement Theory, the research examines reading engagement's behavioral, cognitive, affective, and social dimensions. Over 6 weeks, 16 students participated in small‐group book clubs outside regular school hours, complementing Tier 2 interventions and a Structured Literacy curriculum. Using a quasi‐experimental design, pre‐ and post‐survey data were collected via the Reading Engagement Scale. Results showed positive gains across all engagement dimensions, with behavioral and affective engagement demonstrating the most growth, and cognitive engagement ranking highest overall. The study highlights the effectiveness of student‐centered, balanced literacy approaches in fostering deeper reading engagement, leveraging unused literacy resources to create meaningful learning experiences. All participants met state and classroom assessment goals, underscoring the potential of Book Clubs as a low‐cost intervention for Title 1 schools.

title: From Barriers to Bridges: Promoting Multilingual Language Development Through Parent‐Teacher Collaborations in Early Childhood
text_snippet: From Barriers to Bridges: Promoting Multilingual Language Development Through Parent‐Teacher Collaborations in Early Childhood ABSTRACT This article describes how early childhood teachers can partner with culturally and linguistically diverse families to support the early language and literacy development of emergent bilinguals, specifically for pre‐kindergarten to first‐grade students. The article positions families as valued partners in children's learning and introduces three partnership roles: teachers and families as learners, knowledge‐sharers, and co‐facilitators of home learning. Practical examples show how everyday routines, guided play, and back‐and‐forth conversations in families’ home languages can strengthen bilingual development while building meaningful home–school connections. The article also highlights the role schools and teachers play in creating the structures and supports needed to sustain these partnerships.

title: An Enhanced Science of Reading for Multilingual Learners: The Importance of Leveraging Multilingualism
text_snippet: An Enhanced Science of Reading for Multilingual Learners: The Importance of Leveraging Multilingualism ABSTRACT In this article, the authors re‐examine the Science of Reading (SOR) through the lens of multilingual students (MLs), highlighting the results from a recent review of research that identifies key reading components and effective instructional strategies. They share an overview of results from the review, including the importance of MLs' home languages for developing English reading proficiency and comprehension. Practical strategies such as cognate instruction and a Preview‐View‐Review (P‐V‐R) approach are presented to help educators leverage students' multilingualism, fostering inclusive, responsive classrooms and enhancing English literacy outcomes for MLs. The article offers classroom‐ready examples and addresses common roadblocks teachers face when incorporating home language use into instruction. By bridging research and practice, the authors emphasize the need to expand SOR implementation in ways that affirm linguistic diversity and promote equitable literacy development for all learners.

title: Teaching Reading as a Complex and Multidimensional Process
text_snippet: Teaching Reading as a Complex and Multidimensional Process ABSTRACT This article examines the teaching of reading as a complex and multidimensional process amidst current approaches to teaching reading forwarded by new legislation and curricula that have been adopted across the United States. We underscore the importance of a comprehensive understanding of the teaching of early reading by bringing together five lenses that draw upon a variety of disciplinary perspectives: cognitive, social, culturally sustaining, bi/multilingual, and digital/multimodal. We then examine a small group reading lesson in a second‐grade classroom that is a part of a content area study on global climate justice literacies to show how each of the lenses was employed through students' and teachers' actions in reading instruction. We conclude with a discussion and implications of using these five lenses simultaneously to understand the practice of teaching reading effectively and equitably in today's classrooms.

title: Students Defining Cultural Relevance: Learning From Text Selection in Bilingual Book Clubs
text_snippet: Students Defining Cultural Relevance: Learning From Text Selection in Bilingual Book Clubs ABSTRACT This study explored culturally relevant literacy instruction through bilingual book clubs with Latinx fourth and fifth graders at a dual‐language elementary school. Using the framework of culturally relevant pedagogy—academic success, cultural competence, and critical consciousness—we examined students' responses to Spanish‐English bilingual picturebooks by Latinx authors. Analysis of book discussions revealed how students connected with texts and how facilitators either supported or missed chances for deeper engagement. Cultural relevance goes beyond matching books to cultural labels and should instead reflect students' experiences. Some texts sparked personal and critical conversations on racism, immigration, and language, while others fell flat, highlighting the complexity of Latinidad. This study emphasizes the role of student voice in cultural relevance and calls for a more nuanced view of culture in literacy instruction.

title: From Decoding to Understanding: Building Background Knowledge and Inferencing Skills in Early Readers
text_snippet: From Decoding to Understanding: Building Background Knowledge and Inferencing Skills in Early Readers ABSTRACT This article explores the vital but often overlooked role of inferencing in early reading comprehension. While foundational decoding skills such as phonological awareness and fluency are essential, reading comprehension depends equally on children's ability to construct meaning beyond the words on the page. Drawing on the Simple View of Reading and Scarborough's Reading Rope , the article highlights the importance of background knowledge and verbal reasoning in supporting young readers to make inferences. It introduces the BUILD framework, a practical model for classroom instruction that integrates background knowledge, vocabulary, and inferential thinking into everyday teaching. Through a range of developmentally appropriate strategies, from visual art analysis to intentional read‐alouds, the article illustrates how educators can nurture inferencing from the earliest years. By shifting focus from decoding alone to the broader goal of meaning‐making, it advocates for a more intentional approach to supporting inferencing in the early years.

title: Universal Screeners for Dyslexia: Where is the Spelling?
text_snippet: Universal Screeners for Dyslexia: Where is the Spelling? ABSTRACT Given the integral role spelling plays in literacy development, it would be expected that universal dyslexia screeners include a spelling component. This analysis aimed to determine if spelling is included in commonly used universal dyslexia screeners throughout the United States. We found only 45% (9/20) of the universal dyslexia screeners for kindergarten–Grade 3 include a spelling measure. When spelling measures were included, they were always included in Grade 1 and least likely to be included at the kindergarten level. Results also indicate that phonetically regular words and a correct/incorrect scoring metric are used most frequently. Only one screener included spelling progress monitoring forms. This study provides a synthesis of the status of spelling measures in literacy screeners widely used in the U.S. Educators, researchers, and policymakers can utilize this comprehensive information to make informed decisions when creating, approving, selecting, administering, and/or interpreting universal dyslexia screeners.

title: Not Magic but Manageable: Generative AI and Instructional Decision‐Making in Structured Reading Intervention
text_snippet: Not Magic but Manageable: Generative AI and Instructional Decision‐Making in Structured Reading Intervention ABSTRACT Planning reading interventions often calls for working within a research‐aligned program while tailoring instruction for student needs. We explored how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support educators in reading intervention planning by examining how two novice teachers in a university‐based intervention program used GenAI tools to generate materials, customize texts, and refine lessons. Using the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework and a sociocognitive lens, we examined how teachers' use of GenAI evolved from basic prompting to strategic pedagogical reasoning. Planning became a space for professional learning, where tutors honed content and pedagogical understanding, refined decision‐making, and grew more confident in instructional adaptation. When embedded in collaborative systems, GenAI use surfaced instructional judgment and supported responsive adaptation, though it did not replace the need for human oversight. We offer implications for teacher educators, interventionists, and school leaders seeking to integrate GenAI in ways that strengthen pedagogical growth and instructional responsiveness.

title: Linguistic Patterns in Dual‐Language Books: Strategies to Shape Meaning‐Making for Multilingual Readers
text_snippet: Linguistic Patterns in Dual‐Language Books: Strategies to Shape Meaning‐Making for Multilingual Readers ABSTRACT Multilingual readers use strategies other than phoneme‐grapheme and word patterns to pronounce and comprehend sight words presented in popular children's books. Using the Contemporary Children's High‐Frequency Words (CCHFW) list, which represents culturally and linguistically diverse and inclusive words, this article provides resources and translanguaging instructional strategies to support language transfer in a contextual setting and high‐frequency word instruction for multilingual and monolingual learners' reading development. Using excerpts from four children's texts written by Latinx authors, this article demonstrates decoding practices through the support of four linguistic patterns (borrowed language, cognates, transfer of sounds, and directly incorporated words).

title: Stories and Sequences: Supporting Computational Thinking Through Literacy in Early Childhood
text_snippet: Stories and Sequences: Supporting Computational Thinking Through Literacy in Early Childhood ABSTRACT Early literacy experiences, including reading and writing, serve as meaningful backdrops for teachers in early childhood contexts to support and embed both computational thinking and computer science into classroom instruction. This article shares how interactive in‐class instruction that is embedded within rich literacy experiences and computer science concepts allow young children to think deeply about books that are read to them and engage in forms of creative composition. Examples of common children's books are used to demonstrate and provide opportunities for children to develop early comprehension and composition skills that intersect with computational thinking skills and computer science competencies in naturalistic and unplugged classroom contexts.

title: The Importance of Adaptive Literacy Instruction: Now More Than Ever
text_snippet: The Importance of Adaptive Literacy Instruction: Now More Than Ever ABSTRACT Decades of research demonstrate that adaptive teaching enhances student literacy achievement. We conducted a study to investigate occurrences of adaptive teaching and the reflection process of one expert teacher during literacy instruction. We observed lessons using the Adaptive Teaching Observation Protocol (ATOP) and interviewed the teacher after each observed lesson. Our findings show that the teacher demonstrated a high level of responsiveness by making several unplanned instructional adaptations during lessons. This manuscript offers descriptive examples of adaptive teaching to illustrate how teachers integrate research‐based instruction (i.e., science of reading [SoR]) to effectively meet the literacy needs of all learners in today's diverse classrooms.

title: Preparing Young Children for the Digital World: Engaging Elementary Learners in Digital‐Centered Pedagogy Without Screens
text_snippet: Preparing Young Children for the Digital World: Engaging Elementary Learners in Digital‐Centered Pedagogy Without Screens ABSTRACT As digital media consumption becomes an integral part of children's lives, early literacy education must evolve to include foundational contemporary literacy skills. While traditional literacy instruction focuses on reading, writing, and comprehension, young learners also need conceptual knowledge about digital media and literacy before engaging with screens independently. This article examines how elementary educators can integrate age‐appropriate digital literacy concepts into instruction without increasing screen time. Drawing on frameworks for digital and social media literacy, we explore practical classroom strategies, including interactive read‐alouds, unplugged coding activities, and participatory discussions, to foster critical thinking and problem‐solving skills in the digital age. Through the case study of an elementary educator integrating these approaches in a library and makerspace setting, we demonstrate how early exposure to digital concepts can support students' future engagement with technology in a developmentally appropriate manner. By embedding these skills into foundational literacy instruction, educators can help young children navigate an increasingl

title: Building Thinking Classrooms in Literacy: Collaborative Semantic Gradients for Grades 2–7 Content Reading
text_snippet: Building Thinking Classrooms in Literacy: Collaborative Semantic Gradients for Grades 2–7 Content Reading ABSTRACT Connecting explicit vocabulary study to movement, talk, and shared decision‐making offers a potent yet often untapped route to deeper reading comprehension in the middle elementary years. This article describes a concise routine—semantic gradients enacted by visibly random triads on vertical non‐permanent surfaces—that fuses embodied learning with collaborative word study. Although ranking words along a continuum is a well‐researched practice, coupling it with Liljedahl's (2014) random grouping and upright whiteboards is seldom seen in literacy blocks beyond quick “word‐of‐the‐day” drills. This article analyzes the key structural features of the routine—public group formation, standing work, and photographic retrieval—and illustrates its use in a Grade 3–4 classroom where multilingual and neurodiverse learners jointly negotiated the meanings of content‐area terms. By unpacking design principles and practical adaptations, the article invites teachers to adopt this accessible tool for cultivating inclusive, high‐impact word learning.

title: Exploring Children's Voices on Picture Books Through the Lens of Joy
text_snippet: Exploring Children's Voices on Picture Books Through the Lens of Joy ABSTRACT This study aims to understand how young children interpret picture books, highlighting their authentic voices through Gholdy Muhammad's Unearthing Joy framework (2023). Using teacher–child discussions ( n = 41) and children's drawings ( n = 40), we explore how children aged 36–74 months construct identity, build skills, engage intellectually, think critically, and experience joy through picture books. Our findings show that children can connect stories to their experiences, such as distinguishing real fears from fictional safety, and creatively reimagining stories supported by children's drawings. By centering children's perspectives, we highlight their agency in shaping literary experiences and offer insights for educators to enhance early learning through joy‐centered literacy practices.
