title: Promoting Fluency Through Challenge: Repeated Reading With Texts of Varying Complexity
text_snippet: Promoting Fluency Through Challenge: Repeated Reading With Texts of Varying Complexity ABSTRACT Fluency is a central tenet of productive reading and shares a complex relationship with other reading processes such as reading comprehension, vocabulary, language, and executive functioning. Supporting fluency for upper elementary readers entails unique considerations. In this article, the authors detail how the authors designed an adolescent fluency protocol and piloted it with fourth grade students. Central tenets of the protocol included repeated reading, wide reading, and reading texts of varying complexity. Finally, the authors share the results of the pilot and implications for classroom instruction.

title: Sequencing Nursery Rhymes Through Early Coding in Preschool Settings
text_snippet: Sequencing Nursery Rhymes Through Early Coding in Preschool Settings ABSTRACT Employment in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields will continue to grow in the coming years. Those entering the STEM workforce will be expected to demonstrate proficiency in areas such as literacy and problem solving, among other domains. Early access to STEM concepts such as coding may support skill development and foundational interests. This small project involved in integrating early coding concepts with foundational literacy skills in a preschool classroom setting through the use of nursery rhymes to promote both literacy and coding sequencing skills. Through lessons involving grids, directional arrows, and story character game pieces, students practiced sequencing events while learning basic coding vocabulary. Pre‐ and post‐assessments revealed that preschool students demonstrated improvements in sequencing skills and began developing an emerging understanding of foundational early coding vocabulary. This suggests promising potential for integrating early coding concepts into early childhood curricula.

title: Ready, Set for Variability, Read!
text_snippet: Ready, Set for Variability, Read! ABSTRACT In printed English, there is some variability in the relationships between graphemes and the phonemes they represent. Learners who are sensitive to this variability learn to adjust their attempted pronunciation of an unfamiliar word such that they identify a real word that fits the context. This sensitivity and the ability to adjust attempted pronunciations are referred to as Set for Variability (SfV). Readers with a well‐developed SfV try out different, reasonable pronunciations for graphemes in unfamiliar words and confirm accuracy by matching the decoding attempt to a word in their oral vocabularies and/or ensuring their attempted word makes sense in context. In this article, we discuss the research behind SfV and present instructional suggestions for developing SfV in young readers.

title: Establishing “Selfhood”—A Book Club, Community‐Based Theater and Literary Interpretations
text_snippet: Establishing “Selfhood”—A Book Club, Community‐Based Theater and Literary Interpretations ABSTRACT This article describes research on the Harbor Us Book Club. Critical analysis of the reading responses from preteen Black youth remains surprisingly rare in literacy studies. Our inquiry asks: How do readers develop literary and lived understandings of selfhood in response to the books? In what follows, we describe the theoretical frameworks and research methods undergirding this project. We then present two themes exemplifying our key findings and conclude with implications for schools and communities.

title: Bringing Literacy Into Bilingual Science: Using Cognitive Discourse Functions to Support Reading and Writing in English as a Foreign Language Classrooms
text_snippet: Bringing Literacy Into Bilingual Science: Using Cognitive Discourse Functions to Support Reading and Writing in English as a Foreign Language Classrooms ABSTRACT In bilingual elementary classrooms where English is taught as a foreign language, science lessons often prioritize spoken interaction, while reading and writing receive less emphasis. This article explores how Cognitive Discourse Functions (CDFs)—such as defining, explaining, hypothesizing, and evaluating—can support disciplinary and interdisciplinary literacy development by integrating English language use into content learning. Drawing on three classroom vignettes from public schools in Taiwan, the article illustrates how science teachers designed lessons that help students read scientific texts, write lab reports, and engage in structured discussions—all in English. Practical guidelines are provided to help K–6 educators incorporate reading and writing into bilingual science instruction, with an emphasis on multimodal scaffolding and English academic language development. The paper highlights how CDFs can serve as a bridge between content and language learning, helping students deepen their understanding of scientific concepts while also building the literacy skills needed to think and communicate like scientists in English.

title: Reading Side by Side: A Second‐Grade Teacher's Inquiry Into Dyad Partner Reading
text_snippet: Reading Side by Side: A Second‐Grade Teacher's Inquiry Into Dyad Partner Reading ABSTRACT Fluency is a key component of recent literacy legislation in most US states, and these mandates often require regular assessments to identify at‐risk students and monitor growth, including measures of reading fluency. This classroom inquiry examined how dyad partner reading was implemented and its impact on 19 second‐grade students' words per minute during 9 weeks of daily 10‐min sessions. The partner reading routine produced overall gains in reading rate and revealed patterns in the types of support learners needed to progress. Implementation insights also emerged, including the importance of explicit routine teaching, thoughtful partner formation, responsive adjustments, and attention to partner dynamics. These findings suggest that brief, daily dyad partner reading can be a practical fluency intervention within instructional frameworks and highlight implementation lessons that may help teachers apply the routine effectively.

title: Translanguaging Pedagogy and Testimonios: Reading and Teaching Latinx Children's Literature
text_snippet: Translanguaging Pedagogy and Testimonios: Reading and Teaching Latinx Children's Literature ABSTRACT Amidst xenophobia, censorship, and challenges to curricula that represent the global majority, it is necessary to advocate for and cultivate translanguaging literacies as we seek linguistic justice in all classrooms. In this article, we use translanguaging and testimonios as pedagogical tools rooted in social justice to explore the experiences of reading teachers and their students as they study the intersections of language and identity in Latinx children's literature. We detail the moves from a professional learning series centered on a “writing for desahogo” framework that integrates multimodal texts for reading and writing, and we put these into conversation with a district‐level application from the perspective of a Multilingual English Language Learner Service Administrator. We explain the origin of this collaboration between a researcher and a practitioner, describe lessons that use Latinx children's literature for reading and language analysis, and explain how to implement and adapt them for English‐language and bilingual classrooms. title: Spit Your Truth, Write Your Power
text_snippet: Spit Your Truth, Write Your Power ABSTRACT This article details how four literacy educators used the concept of remixing to transform the writing classroom. We share composite student portraits that illustrate real instructional encounters from our collective teaching experiences. Alongside structured activities, personal reflections and practical guidance, we showcase how educators can begin to reimagine their writing instruction as a space that fosters linguistic justice.

title: Using the Yellow River Challenge to Integrate Literacy and Engineering in a Multilingual Third‐Grade Classroom: Taking Initial Steps Toward Translanguaging
text_snippet: Using the Yellow River Challenge to Integrate Literacy and Engineering in a Multilingual Third‐Grade Classroom: Taking Initial Steps Toward Translanguaging ABSTRACT Engineering design challenges offer a potentially rich site for providing learning opportunities for emergent bilingual and multilingual learners. This intrinsic case study demonstrates how Emily, a third‐grade teacher and co‐author on this article, integrated literacy and engineering during a social studies unit about China. The authors illustrate how Emily facilitated the engineering design process while integrating literacy practices and how she took small steps toward translanguaging and strategies to support students in her diverse, multilingual classroom. Findings demonstrate how Emily took initial steps toward introducing engineering and translanguaging despite being a monolingual teacher with no background in engineering and document where Emily feels she needs to continue developing. The article suggests that teachers can implement engineering design with a translanguaging stance, design, and shifts in elementary classrooms.

title: Day of the Dead as a Forum for Grief Education and Literacy Learning
text_snippet: Day of the Dead as a Forum for Grief Education and Literacy Learning ABSTRACT Teachers are uniquely positioned to educate about grief, but we do not always know how. Drawing from findings of a qualitative research study, this article describes how K‐5 teachers provide literacy lessons connected to the Day of the Dead. Examples include opinion writing, analyzing characters, and comparing concepts in informational texts. Importantly, lessons engage students in discovering diverse and healthy ways to grieve loss, which may include losing a loved one or losing one's homeland. This article shows how teachers can foster thinking, reading, and writing about a topic that is difficult, critical, humanizing, and universal.

title: Are Palestinian Children Beautiful Too?: Islamic View of Beauty in Picture Books About Palestine and Palestinians
text_snippet: Are Palestinian Children Beautiful Too?: Islamic View of Beauty in Picture Books About Palestine and Palestinians ABSTRACT The ongoing genocide in Palestine is a challenging topic for many teachers, who remain silent to avoid being labeled antisemitic. Children's literature centered on the Islamic view of beauty (soul, body, action, Deen) can help teachers focus on the beauty of Palestinian children and foster empathy and global connection.
